Arab world
The Arab world comprises a large group of countries, mainly located in <color=#3366CC>West Asia</color> and <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color>. While the majority
of people in the Arab world are ethnically Arab, there are also significant populations of other ethnic groups such as

<color=#3366CC>Berbers</color>, <color=#3366CC>Kurds</color>, Somalis and Nubians, among other groups. <color=#3366CC>Arabic</color> is used as the <color=#3366CC>lingua franca</color> throughout the Arab
world.
The Arab world is usually defined as the 19 states where Arabs form at least a of the population. At its maximum
defination it consists of the 22 members of the <color=#3366CC>Arab League</color>, an international organization, which on top of the 19

plurality Arab states also includes the <color=#3366CC>Bantu</color>-speaking <color=#3366CC>Comoros</color>, and the Cushitic-speaking <color=#3366CC>Djibouti</color> and <color=#3366CC>Somalia</color>. The
region stretches from the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic Ocean</color> in the west to the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Sea</color> in the east, and from the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color> in
the north to the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean</color> in the southeast. The eastern part of the Arab world is known as the Mashriq, and the
western part as the <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color>.
According to the <color=#3366CC>World Bank</color>, the Arab world has a total population of 456 million inhabitants and a <color=#3366CC>gross domestic</color>
<color=#3366CC>product</color> of $2.85 trillion, as of 2021. The region is economically quite diverse, and includes some of the wealthiest as
well as poorest populations in the world.
In <color=#3366CC>post-classical history</color>, the Arab world was synonymous with the historic Arab empires and caliphates. Arab
nationalism arose in the second half of the 19th century along with other nationalist movements within the <color=#3366CC>Ottoman</color>
<color=#3366CC>Empire</color>. The Arab League was formed in 1945 to represent the interests of Arab people and especially to pursue the
political unification of the Arab countries, a project known as pan-Arabism.
Terminology
In page 9 of Best Divisions for Knowledge of the Regions, 10th century Arab geographer Al Maqdisi used the term Arab
regions to refer to the lands of the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Peninsula</color> (Bahrain, Iraq, Jordan, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia,
United Arab Emirates and Yemen). He also considered Iraq, alongside Upper Mesopotamia (Iraq, Syria and Turkey),
Ash-Sham (Israel, Jordan, Lebanon, Palestine, Syria and Turkey), Egypt and the Maghreb (Algeria, Libya, Mauritania,
Morocco, Tunisia and Western Sahara Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic) to be part of the Arab regions.
<color=#3366CC>Malta</color>, an island country in <color=#3366CC>Southern Europe</color> whose national language, <color=#3366CC>Maltese</color>, derives from Arabic through
SiculoArabic, is not included in the Arab world. Similarly, <color=#3366CC>Chad</color>, <color=#3366CC>Eritrea</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Israel</color> recognize Arabic as one of their
official or working languages but are not included in the region because they are not members of the <color=#3366CC>Arab League</color>.
Definition
The linguistic and political denotation inherent in the term <color=#3366CC>Arab</color> is generally dominant over <color=#3366CC>genealogical</color> considerations.
In Arab states, <color=#3366CC>Standard Arabic</color> is used by the government. Local vernacular languages are referred to as <color=#3366CC>Darija</color> (
"everyday/colloquial language") in the <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color> or Aammiyya ( "common language") in the Mashreq. The majority of
the vocabulary in these vernaculars is shared with Standard Arabic; however, some of them also significantly borrow
from other languages, such as <color=#3366CC>Berber</color>, <color=#3366CC>French</color>, <color=#3366CC>Spanish</color> and <color=#3366CC>Italian</color> in the Maghreb.
Standard territorial
Although no globally accepted definition of the Arab world exists, all countries that are members of the <color=#3366CC>Arab League</color> are
generally acknowledged as being part of the Arab world.
The Arab League is a regional organisation that aims, among other things, to consider in a general way the affairs and
interests of the Arab countries and sets out the following definition of an Arab:
An Arab is a person whose language is Arabic, who lives in an Arab country, and who is in sympathy with the
aspirations of the Arab people.
This standard territorial definition is sometimes seen to be inappropriate or problematic, and may be supplemented with
certain additional elements (see ancillary linguistic definition below).
Member states of the Arab League
Ancillary linguistic
As an alternative to, or in combination with, the standard territorial definition, the Arab world may be defined as
consisting of peoples and states united to at least some degree by Arabic language, culture or geographic contiguity, or
those states or territories in which the majority of the population speaks Arabic, and thus may also include populations
of the Arab diaspora.
When an ancillary linguistic definition is used in combination with the standard territorial definition, various parameters
may be applied to determine whether a state or territory should be included in this alternative definition of the Arab
world. These parameters may be applied to the states and territories of the Arab League (which constitute the Arab
world under the standard definition) and to other states and territories. Typical parameters that may be applied include:
whether Arabic is widely spoken; whether Arabic is an official or national language; or whether an Arabic cognate
language is widely spoken.
While Arabic dialects are spoken in a number of Arab League states, <color=#3366CC>Literary Arabic</color> is official in all of them. Several
states have declared Arabic to be an official or national language, although Arabic is not as widely spoken there. As
members of the Arab League, however, they are considered part of the Arab world under the standard territorial
definition.

<color=#3366CC>Somalia</color> has two official languages, Arabic and <color=#3366CC>Somali</color>, while <color=#3366CC>Somaliland</color> has three, Arabic, Somali and <color=#3366CC>English</color>. Both
Arabic and Somali belong to the larger <color=#3366CC>Afro-Asiatic</color> language family. Although Arabic is widely spoken by many people
in the north and urban areas in the south, Somali is the most widely used language, and contains many Arabic <color=#3366CC>loan</color>
<color=#3366CC>words</color>.
Similarly, <color=#3366CC>Djibouti</color> has two official languages, Arabic and <color=#3366CC>French</color>. It also has several formally recognized national
languages; besides Somali, many people speak <color=#3366CC>Afar</color>, which is also an Afro-Asiatic language. The majority of the
population speaks Somali and Afar, although Arabic is also widely used for trade and other activities.
The <color=#3366CC>Comoros</color> has three official languages: Arabic, Comorian and French. Comorian is the most widely spoken
language, with Arabic having a religious significance, and French being associated with the educational system.
<color=#3366CC>Chad</color>, <color=#3366CC>Eritrea</color> and <color=#3366CC>Israel</color> all recognize Arabic as an official or working language, but none of them is a member-state of
the Arab League, although both Chad and Eritrea are observer states of the League (with possible future membership)
and have large populations of Arabic speakers.
Israel is not a part of the Arab world. By some definitions, Arab citizens of Israel may concurrently be considered a
constituent part of the Arab world.
<color=#3366CC>Iran</color> has about 1.5 million Arabic speakers. Iranian Arabs are mainly found in <color=#3366CC>Ahvaz</color>, a southwestern region in the

<color=#3366CC>Khuzestan Province</color>; others inhabit the <color=#3366CC>Bushehr</color> and <color=#3366CC>Hormozgan</color> provinces and the city of <color=#3366CC>Qom</color>. <color=#3366CC>Mali</color> and <color=#3366CC>Senegal</color>
recognize Hassaniya, the Arabic dialect of the <color=#3366CC>Moorish</color> ethnic minority, as a national language. <color=#3366CC>Greece</color> and <color=#3366CC>Cyprus</color> also
recognize Cypriot Maronite Arabic under the European Charter for Regional or Minority Languages. Additionally, Malta,
though not part of the Arab world, has as its official language <color=#3366CC>Maltese</color>. The language is grammatically akin to Maghrebi
Arabic.
History
Early history
The <color=#3366CC>Arabs</color> historically originate as a Central Semitic group in the northern <color=#3366CC>Arabian Peninsula</color>, the Southern Levant and
the <color=#3366CC>Syrian Desert</color>. Arab tribes and federations included the Nabataeans, Tanukhids, Salihids, <color=#3366CC>Ghassanids</color>.

Arab expansion is due to the <color=#3366CC>early Muslim conquests</color> of the 7th and 8th centuries. <color=#3366CC>Iraq</color> was <color=#3366CC>conquered</color> in 633, <color=#3366CC>Levant</color>
(modern Syria, Israel, Palestine, Jordan and Lebanon) was <color=#3366CC>conquered</color> between 636 and 640 CE. Egypt was <color=#3366CC>conquered</color>
in 639, and gradually Arabized during the medieval period. A distinctively <color=#3366CC>Egyptian Arabic</color> language emerged by the
16th century. The <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color> was also <color=#3366CC>conquered</color> in the 7th century, and gradually Arabized under the <color=#3366CC>Fatimids</color>. Islam
was brought to <color=#3366CC>Sudan</color> from Egypt during the 8th to 11th centuries. The culture of Sudan today depends on the tribe,
some have a pure Nubian, Beja, or Arabic culture and some have a mixture of Arab and Nubian elements.
Ottoman and colonial rule
The Arab <color=#3366CC>Abbasid Caliphate</color> fell to the <color=#3366CC>Mongol invasions</color> in the 13th century. Egypt, the Levant and Hejaz also came
under the Turkish <color=#3366CC>Mamluk Sultanate</color>.
By 1570, the Turkish <color=#3366CC>Ottoman Empire</color> controlled most of the Arab world. However, <color=#3366CC>Morocco</color> remained under the rule of
the Zenata Wattasid dynasty, which was succeeded by the <color=#3366CC>Saadi dynasty</color> in the 16th to 17th centuries. The <color=#3366CC>Ajuran</color>
<color=#3366CC>Sultanate</color> also held sway in the southern part of the Horn region.
The sentiment of Arab nationalism arose in the second half of the 19th century along with other nationalisms within the
declining Ottoman Empire.
When the Ottoman Empire collapsed as a result of <color=#3366CC>World War I</color>, much of the Arab world came to be controlled by the
European colonial empires: Mandatory Palestine, Mandatory Iraq, British protectorate of Egypt, French protectorate of
Morocco, Italian Libya, <color=#3366CC>French Tunisia</color>, <color=#3366CC>French Algeria</color>, Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon and the so-called Trucial
States, a British protectorate formed by the sheikhdoms on the former "Pirate Coast".
These Arab states only gained their independence during or after <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>: the <color=#3366CC>Republic of Lebanon</color> in 1943, the
<color=#3366CC>Syrian Arab Republic</color> and the <color=#3366CC>Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan</color> in 1946, the Kingdom of Libya in 1951, the Kingdom of
Egypt in 1952, the <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Morocco</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tunisia</color> in 1956, the <color=#3366CC>Republic of Iraq</color> in 1958, the Somali Republic in 1960,
<color=#3366CC>Algeria</color> in 1962, and the <color=#3366CC>United Arab Emirates</color> in 1971.
By contrast, <color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabia</color> had fragmented with the fall of the Ottoman Empire, and was <color=#3366CC>unified</color> under <color=#3366CC>Ibn Saud of Saudi</color>
<color=#3366CC>Arabia</color> by 1932.
The Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen also seceded directly from the Ottoman Empire in 1918. <color=#3366CC>Oman</color>, apart from brief
intermittent Persian and Portuguese rule, has been self-governing since the 8th century.
Rise of Arab nationalism
The Arab League was formed in 1945 to represent the interests of the Arabs, and especially to pursue the political
unification of the Arab world, a project known as Pan-Arabism. There were some short-lived attempts at such
unification in the mid-20th century, notably the United Arab Republic of 1958 to 1961. The Arab League's main goal is
to unify politically the Arab populations so defined. Its permanent headquarters are located in <color=#3366CC>Cairo</color>. However, it was
moved temporarily to <color=#3366CC>Tunis</color> during the 1980s, after Egypt was expelled for signing the Camp David Accords (1978).
Pan-Arabism has mostly been abandoned as an ideology since the 1980s, and was replaced by Pan-Islamism on one
hand, and individual nationalisms on the other.
Modern conflicts
Unification of Saudi Arabia
The <color=#3366CC>unification of Saudi Arabia</color> was a 30-year-long military and political campaign, by which the various <color=#3366CC>tribes</color>,
sheikhdoms, and emirates of most of the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Peninsula</color> were conquered by the <color=#3366CC>House of Saud</color>, or Al Saud,
between 1902 and 1932, when the modern-day <color=#3366CC>Kingdom of Saudi Arabia</color> was proclaimed. Carried out under the
charismatic <color=#3366CC>Abdul Aziz Ibn Saud</color>, this process created what is sometimes referred to as the Third Saudi State, to
differentiate it from the first and second states that existed under the Al Saud clan.
The Al-Saud had been in exile in Ottoman Iraq since 1893 following the disintegration of the Second Saudi State and
the rise of Jebel Shammar under the Al Rashid clan. In 1902, Ibn Saud recaptured <color=#3366CC>Riyadh</color>, the Al Saud dynasty's

former capital. He went on to subdue the rest of <color=#3366CC>Nejd</color>, <color=#3366CC>Al-Hasa</color>, Jebel Shammar, <color=#3366CC>Asir</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Hejaz</color> (location of the <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color>
holy cities of <color=#3366CC>Mecca</color> and <color=#3366CC>Medina</color>) between 1913 and 1926. The resultant polity was named the Kingdom of Nejd and
Hejaz from 1927 until it was further consolidated with Al-Hasa and <color=#3366CC>Qatif</color> into the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia in 1932.
Arab–Israeli conflict
The establishment of the <color=#3366CC>State of Israel</color> in 1948 has given rise to the <color=#3366CC>Arab–Israeli conflict</color>, one of the major unresolved
geopolitical conflicts.
The Arab states in changing alliances were involved in a number of wars with Israel and its western allies between

1948 and 1973, including the <color=#3366CC>1948 Arab–Israeli War</color>, the 1956 <color=#3366CC>Suez Crisis</color>, the <color=#3366CC>Six-Day War</color> of 1967, and the <color=#3366CC>Yom</color>
<color=#3366CC>Kippur War</color> of 1973. An Egypt–Israel peace treaty was signed in 1979.
Iran–Iraq War
The <color=#3366CC>Iran–Iraq War</color> (also known as the First Gulf War and by various other names) was an armed conflict between the
armed forces of Iraq and Iran, lasting from September 1980 to August 1988, making it the second longest conventional
war of the 20th century. It was initially referred to in English as the "Gulf War" prior to the "Gulf War" of 1990.
The war began when Iraq invaded Iran, launching a simultaneous invasion by air and land into Iranian territory on 22
September 1980 following a long history of border disputes, and fears of Shia Islam insurgency among Iraq's
long-suppressed Shia majority influenced by the Iranian Revolution. Iraq was also aiming to replace Iran as the
dominant Persian Gulf state. Although Iraq hoped to take advantage of the revolutionary chaos in Iran (see <color=#3366CC>Iranian</color>
<color=#3366CC>Revolution</color>, 1979) and attacked without formal warning, they made only limited progress into Iran and were quickly
repelled by the Iranians who regained virtually all lost territory by June 1982. For the next six years, Iran was on the
offensive.
Lebanese Civil War
The <color=#3366CC>Lebanese Civil War</color> was a multifaceted civil war in Lebanon, lasting from 1975 to 1990 and resulting in an
estimated 120,000 fatalities. Another one million people (a quarter of the population) were wounded, and today
approximately 76,000 people remain displaced within Lebanon. There was also a mass exodus of almost one million
people from Lebanon.
Western Sahara conflict
The <color=#3366CC>Western Sahara War</color> was an armed struggle between the Sahrawi Polisario Front and Morocco between 1975 and
1991, being the most significant phase of the Western Sahara conflict. The conflict erupted after the withdrawal of
Spain from the Spanish Sahara in accordance with the Madrid Accords, by which it transferred administrative control of
the territory to Morocco and Mauritania, but not the sovereignty. In 1975, Moroccan government organized the Green
March of some 350,000 Moroccan citizens, escorted by around 20,000 troops, who entered Western Sahara, trying to
establish Moroccan presence.
While at first met with just minor resistance by the Polisario, Morocco later engaged a long period of guerilla warfare
with the Sahrawi nationalists. During the late 1970s, the Polisario Front, desiring to establish an independent state in
the territory, successively fought both Mauritania and Morocco. In 1979, Mauritania withdrew from the conflict after
signing a peace treaty with the Polisario. The war continued in low intensity throughout the 1980s, though Morocco
made several attempts to take the upper hand in 1989–1991. A cease-fire agreement was finally reached between the
Polisario Front and Morocco in September 1991.
North Yemen Civil War
The <color=#3366CC>North Yemen Civil War</color> was fought in North Yemen between royalists of the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen and
factions of the Yemen Arab Republic from 1962 to 1970. The war began with a coup d'état carried out by the republican
leader, Abdullah as-Sallal, which dethroned the newly crowned Imam al-Badr and declared Yemen a republic under his
presidency. The Imam escaped to the Saudi Arabian border and rallied popular support.
Somali Civil War
The <color=#3366CC>Somali Civil War</color> is an ongoing civil war taking place in <color=#3366CC>Somalia</color>. It began in 1991, when a coalition of clan-based
armed opposition groups ousted the nation's long-standing military government.
Various factions began competing for influence in the power vacuum that followed, which precipitated an aborted UN
peacekeeping attempt in the mid-1990s. A period of decentralization ensued, characterized by a return to customary
and religious law in many areas as well as the establishment of autonomous regional governments in the northern part
of the country. The early 2000s saw the creation of fledgling interim federal administrations, culminating in the
establishment of the Transitional Federal Government (TFG) in 2004.
In 2006, the TFG, assisted by Ethiopian troops, assumed control of most of the nation's southern conflict zones from
the newly formed Islamic Courts Union (ICU). The ICU splintered into more radical groups, notably Al-Shabaab, which
have since been fighting the Somali government and its AMISOM allies for control of the region. In 2011, a coordinated
military operation between the Somali military and multinational forces began, which is believed to represent one of the
final stages in the war's Islamist insurgency.
Arab Spring
The <color=#3366CC>popular protests throughout the Arab world</color> of late 2010 to the present have been directed against authoritarian
leadership and associated <color=#3366CC>political corruption</color>, paired with demands for more democratic rights. The two most violent
and prolonged conflicts in the aftermath of the Arab Spring are the Libyan Civil War and Syrian Civil War.
Petroleum
While the Arab world had been of limited interest to the European colonial powers, the <color=#3366CC>British Empire</color> being mostly
interested in the <color=#3366CC>Suez Canal</color> as a route to British India, the economic and geopolitical situation changed dramatically
after the discovery of large <color=#3366CC>petroleum</color> deposits in the 1930s, coupled with the vastly increased demand for petroleum in
the west as a result of the <color=#3366CC>Second Industrial Revolution</color>.
The <color=#3366CC>Persian Gulf</color> is particularly well-endowed with this strategic raw material: five Persian Gulf states, Saudi Arabia,
Iraq, the UAE, Kuwait, and Qatar, are among the top ten petroleum or gas exporters worldwide. In Africa, Algeria (10th
world) and Libya are important gas exporters. Bahrain, Egypt, Tunisia, and Sudan all have smaller but significant
reserves. Where present, these have had significant effects on regional politics, often enabling rentier states, leading to
economic disparities between oil-rich and oil-poor countries, and, particularly in the more sparsely populated states of
the Persian Gulf and Libya, triggering extensive labor immigration. It is believed that the Arab world holds
approximately 46% of the world's total proven oil reserves and a quarter of the world's natural-gas reserves.
<color=#3366CC>Islamism</color> and Pan-Islamism were on the rise during the 1980s. The <color=#3366CC>Hezbollah</color>, a militant Islamic party in <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color>, was
founded in 1982. Islamic terrorism became a problem in the Arab world in the 1970s to 1980s. While the <color=#3366CC>Muslim</color>
<color=#3366CC>Brotherhood</color> had been active in Egypt since 1928, their militant actions were limited to assassination attempts on
political leaders.
Recent history
Today, Arab states are characterized by their <color=#3366CC>autocratic rulers</color> and lack of democratic control. The 2016 Democracy

Index classifies <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color>, <color=#3366CC>Iraq</color> and <color=#3366CC>Palestine</color> as "hybrid regimes", <color=#3366CC>Tunisia</color> as a "flawed democracy" and all other Arab
states as "authoritarian regimes". Similarly, the 2011 Freedom House report classifies the <color=#3366CC>Comoros</color> and <color=#3366CC>Mauritania</color> as
"<color=#3366CC>electoral democracies</color>", Lebanon, <color=#3366CC>Kuwait</color> and <color=#3366CC>Morocco</color> as "partly free", and all other Arab states as "not free".

The invasion of Kuwait by Iraq forces, led to the 1990–91 <color=#3366CC>Persian Gulf War</color>. <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, <color=#3366CC>Syria</color> and <color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabia</color> joined a
multinational coalition that opposed Iraq. Displays of support for Iraq by <color=#3366CC>Jordan</color> and <color=#3366CC>Palestine</color> resulted in strained
relations between many of the Arab states. After the war, a so-called "Damascus Declaration" formalized an alliance for
future joint Arab defensive actions between Egypt, Syria, and the GCC states.
A chain of events leading to the destabilization of the authoritarian regimes established during the 1950s throughout the
Arab world became apparent during the early years of the 21st century. The <color=#3366CC>2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq</color> led to the
collapse of the Baathist regime and ultimate execution of Saddam Hussein.
A growing class of young, educated, secular citizens with access to modern media such as <color=#3366CC>Al Jazeera</color> (since 1996)
and communicating via the <color=#3366CC>internet</color> began to form a third force besides the classical dichotomy of Pan-Arabism vs.
Pan-Islamism that had dominated the second half of the 20th century. These citizens wish for reform in their country's
religious institutions.
In Syria, the Damascus Spring of 2000 to 2001 heralded the possibility of democratic change, but the Baathist regime
managed to suppress the movement.
In 2003, the Egyptian Movement for Change, popularly known as Kefaya, was launched to oppose the Mubarak regime
and to establish democratic reforms and greater <color=#3366CC>civil liberties</color> in Egypt.
Geography
The Arab World stretches across more than 13000000 km2 of <color=#3366CC>North Africa</color> and the part of North-East Africa and
South-West Asia. The eastern part of the Arab world is called the Mashriq. Algeria, Morocco, Tunisia, Libya and
Mauritania are the <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color> or Maghrib.
The term "Arab" often connotes the Arabian Peninsula, but the larger (and more populous) part of the Arab World is
North Africa. Its eight million square kilometers include two of the largest countries of the African continent, <color=#3366CC>Algeria</color> (2.4
million km2) in the center of the region and <color=#3366CC>Sudan</color> (1.9 million km2) in the southeast. Algeria is about three-quarters the
size of <color=#3366CC>India</color>, or about one-and-a-half times the size of <color=#3366CC>Alaska</color>, the largest state in the United States. The largest
country in the Arab West Asia is <color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabia</color> (2 million km2).
At the other extreme, the smallest autonomous mainland Arab country is <color=#3366CC>Lebanon</color> (10,452 km2), and the smallest
island Arab country is <color=#3366CC>Bahrain</color> (665 km2).
Every Arab country borders a sea or ocean, with the exception of the Arab region of northern Chad, which is completely
landlocked. Iraq is actually nearly landlocked, as it has only a very narrow access to the Persian Gulf.
Historical boundaries
The political borders of the Arab world have wandered, leaving Arab minorities in non-Arab countries of the <color=#3366CC>Sahel</color> and

the <color=#3366CC>Horn of Africa</color> as well as in the Middle Eastern countries of <color=#3366CC>Cyprus</color>, <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color> and <color=#3366CC>Iran</color>, and also leaving non-Arab
minorities in Arab countries. However, the basic geography of sea, desert and mountain provides the enduring natural
boundaries for this region.
The Arab world straddles two continents, Africa and Asia. It is mainly oriented along an east–west axis.
The West Asian Arab region comprises the <color=#3366CC>Arabian Peninsula</color>, most of the <color=#3366CC>Levant</color> (excluding Cyprus and Israel), most
of Mesopotamia (excluding parts of Turkey and Iran) and the Persian Gulf region. The peninsula is roughly a tilted
rectangle that leans back against the slope of northeast Africa, the long axis pointing toward <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color> and <color=#3366CC>Europe</color>.
Arab North Africa comprises the entire northern third of the continent. It is surrounded by water on three sides (west,
north, and east) and desert or desert scrubland on the fourth (south).
In the west, it is bounded by the shores of the <color=#3366CC>Atlantic Ocean</color>. From northeast to southwest, <color=#3366CC>Morocco</color>, <color=#3366CC>Western Sahara</color>
(mostly unilaterally annexed by Morocco), and <color=#3366CC>Mauritania</color> make up the roughly 2,000 kilometers of Arab Atlantic
coastline. The southwestern sweep of the coast is gentle but substantial, such that Mauritania's capital, <color=#3366CC>Nouakchott</color>
(18°N, 16°W), is far enough west to share longitude with <color=#3366CC>Iceland</color> (13–22°W). Nouakchott is the westernmost capital of
the Arab World and the third-westernmost in Africa, and sits on the Atlantic fringe of the southwestern Sahara. Next
south along the coast from Mauritania is <color=#3366CC>Senegal</color>, whose abrupt border belies the gradient in culture from Arab to
indigenous African that historically characterizes this part of <color=#3366CC>West Africa</color>.
Arab Africa's boundary to the north is again a continental boundary, the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean Sea</color>. This boundary begins in
the west with the narrow <color=#3366CC>Strait of Gibraltar</color>, the thirteen kilometer wide channel that connects the Mediterranean with
the Atlantic to the west, and separates Morocco from <color=#3366CC>Spain</color> to the north. East along the coast from Morocco are
Algeria, Tunisia, and Libya, followed by Egypt, which forms the region's, and the continent's, northeastern corner. The
coast turns briefly but sharply south at Tunisia, slopes more gently southeastward through the Libyan capital of <color=#3366CC>Tripoli</color>,
and bumps north through Libya's second city, <color=#3366CC>Benghazi</color>, before turning straight east again through Egypt's second city,
<color=#3366CC>Alexandria</color>, at the mouth of the Nile. Along with the spine of <color=#3366CC>Italy</color> to its north, Tunisia marks the junction of western and
eastern Mediterranean, and a cultural transition as well: west of Egypt begins the region of the Arab World known as
the <color=#3366CC>Maghreb</color> include (Libya, Tunisia, Algeria, Morocco and Mauritania).
Historically the 4,000-kilometer Mediterranean boundary has fluttered. Population centers north of it in <color=#3366CC>Europe</color> have
invited contact and Arab exploration—mostly friendly, though sometimes not. Islands and peninsulas near the Arab
coast have changed hands. The islands of <color=#3366CC>Sicily</color> and <color=#3366CC>Malta</color> lie just a hundred kilometers east of the Tunisian city of
<color=#3366CC>Carthage</color>, which has been a point of contact with Europe since its founding in the first millennium BCE; both Sicily and
Malta at times have been part of the Arab World. Just across the Strait of Gibraltar from Morocco, regions of the Iberian
peninsula were part of the Arab World throughout the <color=#3366CC>Middle Ages</color>, extending the northern boundary at times to the
foothills of the <color=#3366CC>Pyrenees</color> and leaving a substantial mark on local and wider European and Western culture.
The northern boundary of the African Arab world has also fluttered briefly in the other direction, first through the

<color=#3366CC>Crusades</color> and later through the imperial involvement of <color=#3366CC>France</color>, <color=#3366CC>Britain</color>, <color=#3366CC>Spain</color>, and <color=#3366CC>Italy</color>. Another visitor from northern
shores, <color=#3366CC>Turkey</color>, controlled the east of the region for centuries, though not as a colonizer. Spain still maintains two small
enclaves, <color=#3366CC>Ceuta</color> and <color=#3366CC>Melilla</color> (called "Morocco Espanol"), along the otherwise Moroccan coast. Overall this wave has
ebbed, though like the Arab expansion north it has left its mark. The proximity of North Africa to Europe has always
encouraged interaction, and this continues with Arab immigration to Europe and European interest in the Arab
countries today. However, population centers and the physical fact of the sea keeps this boundary of the Arab World
settled on the Mediterranean coastline.
To the east, the <color=#3366CC>Red Sea</color> defines the boundary between <color=#3366CC>Africa</color> and <color=#3366CC>Asia</color>, and thus also between Arab Africa and Arab
West Asia. This sea is a long and narrow waterway with a northwest tilt, stretching 2,300 kilometers from <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>'s <color=#3366CC>Sinai</color>

<color=#3366CC>Peninsula</color> southeast to the <color=#3366CC>Bab-el-Mandeb</color> strait between <color=#3366CC>Djibouti</color> in Africa and <color=#3366CC>Yemen</color> in Arabia but on average just
150 kilometers wide. Though the sea is navigable along its length, historically much contact between Arab Africa and
Arab West Asia has been either overland across the Sinai or by sea across the Mediterranean or the narrow Bab al
Mendeb strait. From northwest to southeast, Egypt, Sudan, and Eritrea form the African coastline, with Djibouti marking
Bab al Mendeb's African shore.
Southeast along the coast from Djibouti is Somalia, but the Somali coast soon makes a 90-degree turn and heads
northeast, mirroring a bend in the coast of Yemen across the water to the north and defining the south coast of the Gulf
of Aden. The Somali coast then takes a hairpin turn back southwest to complete the horn of Africa. For six months of
the year the <color=#3366CC>monsoon</color> winds blow from up equatorial Somalia, past Arabia and over the small Yemeni archipelago of
<color=#3366CC>Socotra</color>, to rain on <color=#3366CC>India</color>. They then switch directions and blow back.
The east- and especially southeast-coast boundary of Arab Africa has historically been a gateway for maritime trade
and cultural exchange with both <color=#3366CC>East Africa</color> and the subcontinent. The trade winds help explain the presence of the
Comoros islands, an Arab-African country, off the coast of <color=#3366CC>Mozambique</color>, near <color=#3366CC>Madagascar</color> in the <color=#3366CC>Indian Ocean</color>, the
southernmost part of the Arab World.
The southern boundary of Arab North Africa is the strip of scrubland known as the <color=#3366CC>Sahel</color> that crosses the continent
south of the Sahara.
States and territories
For the states and territories constituting the Arab world, see definition above.
Forms of government
Different forms of <color=#3366CC>government</color> are represented in the Arab World: Some of the countries are <color=#3366CC>monarchies</color>: Bahrain,
Jordan, Kuwait, Morocco, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates. The other Arab countries are all
<color=#3366CC>republics</color>. With the exception of Lebanon, Tunisia, Iraq, Palestine, and recently Mauritania, democratic elections
throughout the Arab World are generally viewed as compromised, due to outright vote rigging, intimidation of opposition
parties, and severe restraints on civil liberties and political dissent.
After <color=#3366CC>World War II</color>, Pan-Arabism sought to unite all Arabic-speaking countries into one political entity. Only <color=#3366CC>Syria</color>, <color=#3366CC>Iraq</color>,

<color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>, <color=#3366CC>Sudan</color>, <color=#3366CC>Tunisia</color>, <color=#3366CC>Libya</color> and North Yemen considered the short-lived unification of the United Arab Republic.
Historical divisions, competing local nationalisms, and geographical sprawl were major reasons for the failure of
Pan-Arabism. Arab Nationalism was another strong force in the region which peaked during the mid-20th century and
was professed by many leaders in Egypt, Algeria, Libya, Syria, and Iraq. Arab Nationalist leaders of this period included

<color=#3366CC>Gamal Abdel Nasser</color> of Egypt, <color=#3366CC>Ahmed Ben Bella</color> of Algeria, <color=#3366CC>Michel Aflaq</color>, <color=#3366CC>Salah al-Din al-Bitar</color>, Zaki al-Arsuzi,
Constantin Zureiq and <color=#3366CC>Shukri al-Kuwatli</color> of Syria, <color=#3366CC>Ahmed Hassan al-Bakr</color> of Iraq, <color=#3366CC>Habib Bourguiba</color> of Tunisia, Mehdi
Ben Barka of Morocco, and Shakib Arslan of Lebanon.
Later and current Arab Nationalist leaders include <color=#3366CC>Muammar al-Gaddafi</color> of Libya, <color=#3366CC>Hafez al-Assad</color> and <color=#3366CC>Bashar al-Assad</color>
of Syria. The diverse Arab states generally maintained close ties but distinct national identities developed and
strengthened with the social, historical and political realities of the past 60 years. This has made the idea of a pan-Arab
nation-state increasingly less feasible and likely. Additionally, an upsurge in political Islam has since led to a greater
emphasis on pan-Islamic rather than pan-Arab identity amongst some Arab Muslims. Arab nationalists who once
opposed Islamic movements as a threat to their power, now deal with them differently for reasons of political reality.
Modern boundaries
Many of the modern borders of the Arab World were drawn by <color=#3366CC>European</color> imperial powers during the 19th and early
20th century. However, some of the larger states (in particular <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> and <color=#3366CC>Syria</color>) have historically maintained
geographically definable boundaries, on which some of the modern states are roughly based. The 14th-century
Egyptian historian Al-Maqrizi, for instance, defines Egypt's boundaries as extending from the <color=#3366CC>Mediterranean</color> in the north
to lower <color=#3366CC>Nubia</color> in the south; and between the <color=#3366CC>Red Sea</color> in the east and the oases of the Western/<color=#3366CC>Libyan Desert</color>. The
modern borders of Egypt, therefore, are not a creation of European powers, and are at least in part based on
historically definable entities which are in turn based on certain cultural and ethnic identifications.
At other times, kings, <color=#3366CC>emirs</color> or sheikhs were placed as semi-autonomous rulers over the newly created <color=#3366CC>nation states</color>,
usually chosen by the same imperial powers that for some drew the new borders, for services rendered to European
powers like <color=#3366CC>the British Empire</color>, e.g. <color=#3366CC>Sherif Hussein ibn Ali</color>. Many African states did not attain independence until the
1960s from France after bloody insurgencies for their freedom. These struggles were settled by the imperial powers
approving the form of independence given, so as a consequence almost all of these borders have remained. Some of
these borders were agreed upon without consultation of those individuals that had served the colonial interests of
Britain or France. One such agreement solely between Britain and France (to the exclusion of Sherif Hussein ibn Ali),
signed in total secrecy until <color=#3366CC>Lenin</color> released the full text, was the Sykes-Picot Agreement. Another influential document
written without the consensus of the local population was the <color=#3366CC>Balfour Declaration</color>.
As former director of the Israeli intelligence agency <color=#3366CC>Mossad</color>, Efraim Halevy, now a director at the Hebrew University
said,
The borders, which if you look on the maps of the middle-east are very straight lines, were drawn by British and French
draftsmen who sat with maps and drew the lines of the frontiers with rulers. If the ruler for some reason or other moved
on the map, because of some person's hand shaking, then the frontier moved (with the hand).
He went on to give an example,
There was a famous story about a British consul, a lady named <color=#3366CC>Gertrude Bell</color> who drew the map between Iraq and
Jordan, using transparent paper. She turned to talk to somebody and as she was turning the paper moved and the ruler
moved and that added considerable territory to the (new) Jordanians.
Historian Jim Crow, of Newcastle University, has said:
Without that imperial carve-up, Iraq would not be in the state it is in today...Gertrude Bell was one of two or three
Britons who were instrumental in the creation of the Arab states in the Middle East that were favourable to Britain.
Modern economies
As of 2006, the Arab world accounts for two-fifths of the gross domestic product and three-fifths of the trade of the
wider <color=#3366CC>Muslim world</color>.
The Arab states are mostly, although not exclusively, developing economies and derive their export revenues from oil
and gas, or the sale of other raw materials. Recent years have seen significant economic growth in the Arab World, due
largely to an increase in oil and gas prices, which tripled between 2001 and 2006, but also due to efforts by some
states to diversify their economic base. Industrial production has risen, for example the amount of steel produced
between 2004 and 2005 rose from 8.4 to 19 million tonnes. (Source: Opening speech of Mahmoud Khoudri, <color=#3366CC>Algeria</color>'s
Industry Minister, at the 37th General Assembly of the Iron & Steel Arab Union, Algiers, May 2006). However even 19
million tons pa still only represents 1.7% of global steel production, and remains inferior to the production of countries
like <color=#3366CC>Brazil</color>.
The main economic organisations in the Arab World are the <color=#3366CC>Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC)</color>, comprising the states in
the Persian Gulf, and the Union of the Arab Maghreb (UMA), made up of North African States. The GCC has achieved
some success in financial and monetary terms, including plans to establish a common currency in the Persian Gulf
region. Since its foundation in 1989, the UMA's most significant accomplishment has been the establishment of a 7,000
km highway crossing North Africa from <color=#3366CC>Mauritania</color> to <color=#3366CC>Libya</color>'s border with <color=#3366CC>Egypt</color>. The central stretch of the highway,
expected to be completed in 2010, will cross <color=#3366CC>Morocco</color>, <color=#3366CC>Algeria</color> and <color=#3366CC>Tunisia</color>. In recent years a new term has been
coined to define a greater economic region: the <color=#3366CC>MENA</color> region, standing for "Middle East and North Africa", is becoming
increasingly popular, especially with support from the current US administration.As of August 2009 it was reported that
Saudi Arabia is the strongest Arab economy according to World Bank.
<color=#3366CC>Saudi Arabia</color> remains the top Arab economy in terms of total GDP. It is Asia's eleventh largest economy, followed by
<color=#3366CC>Egypt</color> and <color=#3366CC>Algeria</color>, which were the second and third largest economies in Africa, after <color=#3366CC>South Africa</color>, in 2006. In terms of
GDP per capita, <color=#3366CC>Qatar</color> is the richest developing country in the world.
The total GDP of all Arab countries in 1999 was US$531.2 billion. The total Arab world GDP was estimated to be worth
at least $2.8 trillion in 2011. This is only smaller than the GDP of the US, China, Japan and Germany.
Demographics
In the Arab world, <color=#3366CC>Modern Standard Arabic</color>, derived from <color=#3366CC>Classical Arabic</color> (symptomatic of Arabic <color=#3366CC>diglossia</color>), serves as
an official language in the Arab League states, and Arabic dialects are used as lingua franca. Various indigenous
languages are also spoken, which predate the spread of the Arabic language. This contrasts with the situation in the
wider <color=#3366CC>Islamic world</color>, where, in contiguous Iran, Pakistan and Afghanistan, the <color=#3366CC>Perso-Arabic script</color> is used and Arabic is
the primary liturgical language, but the tongue is not official at the state level or spoken as a vernacular. <color=#3366CC>Arabs</color>
constitute around one quarter of the 1.5 billion <color=#3366CC>Muslims</color> in the Islamic world.
